unit.unitOverview: Say what you do in a usual week at work, or where you study. Say what another person does: she does, he has, it goes. Say what you need to do and what you have finished doing. Ask What is it like? and What is it about?, and answer both.
unit.learningPath:
The lesson: listen and repeat.
Words: listen, look and say. 32 words.
Patterns: 4 cards. Read the one done for you.
Reading: a week, a staff report and a notice.
Speaking: tap the mic. Say it. Listen.
Writing: write about your week. Made-up is OK.
Practice: 6 sets. Check with the answers.
Quiz: 12 questions. At the end, My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
Hello. This is Level 2, Unit 1.
In this unit you talk about your week.
Your week at work, or your week where you study.
First, listen to one person's week.
I work four shifts a week.
My manager makes the shift list on Friday.
She does the list for all the staff.
She has thirty names on one sheet.
It goes on the wall near the door.
Listen again: she does, she has, it goes.
With he, she and it, most words take an s.
work, works. start, starts. prepare, prepares.
But three everyday words change more.
do becomes does. have becomes has. go becomes goes.
Some words take es.
watch, watches. finish, finishes. fix, fixes.
A letter and a y at the end becomes ies.
carry, carries. study, studies. apply, applies.
Say the end clearly. He applies. She finishes.
Only he, she and it change.
I do. We have. They go.
Now, a thing you do not name.
I have something to do before six.
Do you have anything for me?
No, I have nothing today.
Something is for a plain sentence.
Anything is for a question, and after not.
Nothing already has the not inside it.
So say I have nothing, or I do not have anything.
Never put two nots in one line.
For people, use someone, anyone and everyone.
Someone is waiting at the desk.
Is anyone free after four?
Everyone on my shift is new.
These words take the he and she form.
Everyone knows the list. Something goes wrong every week.
Now, two small words. Like, and about.
What is it like? This asks you to describe it.
It is quiet. It is stressful. It is worth the money.
What is it about? This asks for the subject.
It is about money. It is a short book about training.
Like describes. About names the subject.
Last, which word takes to, and which takes ing.
I need to go. I want to apply. We plan to start.
I finish working at eight. I enjoy training new staff.
Need, want, plan, hope, decide and arrange take to.
Finish, enjoy, keep, avoid and practise take ing.
Continue takes both, and the meaning stays the same.
Look at the first word. That word decides.
Now open the words, then the four cards.
Do the practice, then check with the answers.
Then record yourself and listen back.
Your week can be made up. That is fine.

readings.title: Four Shifts a Week
readings.setting: A person writes about a usual week at work.
readings.passageScript:
My name is Lena. My week is not the same every week.
I work four shifts, and my manager makes the shift list on Friday.
She does the list for all the staff. She has thirty names on one sheet.
It goes on the wall near the door.
Everyone looks at it before they go home.
This week I have two early shifts and two late ones.
The early shift is quiet. Nothing happens before eight.
I prepare the room, and I select the boxes for the day.
The late shift is different. It is tiring, and it is never quiet.
A customer always wants something at the end of the day.
On Tuesday I have training. It is about customers and the new phones.
I want to apply for a better job, so the training is worth it.
I finish working at eight, and I study English for one hour at home.
That hour is the best part of my week.

readings.passageScript:
THE STAFF REPORT
Twenty people answered four questions about their work.
1. What is your usual week like?
Eleven said it is normal and quiet. Six said it is tiring. Three said it is stressful.
2. Do you do overtime?
Fourteen do overtime every month. Four do it sometimes. Two never do any.
3. What is the training about?
Most of the training is about customers and the new phones.
Nothing in it is about the wage.
4. Who do you ask when something goes wrong?
Twelve ask a colleague first. Seven ask the manager. One asks the customer.
Everyone wants the same thing: more time to prepare.
Nine people said the deadline is too near.
The manager plans to arrange a new shift list in March.
She hopes to give every shift one quiet hour.

grammar.title: He does, she has, it goes
grammar.explanation:
You know the s after he, she and it: she works.
Three everyday words do not just take an s.
do becomes does. have becomes has. go becomes goes.
The spelling also changes after ch, sh, s and x, and after a letter and y.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The three to learn by heart:
do — he does
have — she has
go — it goes

After ch, sh, s or x, add es:
watch — watches
finish — finishes
pass — passes
fix — fixes

A letter and y becomes ies:
carry — carries
apply — applies
study — studies
But: pay — pays

Most other words just take s:
work — works
prepare — prepares
handle — handles

Only he, she and it change:
I do. We have. They go.

After does and doesn't, no change:
Does she do the shift list?
She doesn't do it on Monday.
grammar.workedExample:
My manager ___ the shift list on Friday. (do)
1. My manager is she or he.
2. With she and he, the word changes.
3. Do is one of the three: it becomes does.
4. My manager does the shift list on Friday.
5. Say it out loud. Does sounds like duz, not doo-s.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to write the plain word after he or she.
No: He have two shifts.
Yes: He has two shifts.
No: She do the shift list.
Yes: She does the shift list.
Read the word at the front of the line first. He, she or it? Then check the end.
grammar.memoryTip: Three to learn by heart: does, has, goes.

3. The last bus ___ at ten. (go)
4. He ___ his shift at eight. (finish)

1. does  2. has  3. goes  4. finishes  5. carries  6. applies  7. opens  8. takes

grammar.title: Something, anything, nothing
grammar.explanation:
Use these words when you do not name the thing or the person.
Something is for a plain sentence.
Anything is for a question, and for a sentence with not.
Nothing already has the not inside it.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A thing:
I have something to do. (plain sentence)
Do you need anything? (question)
I don't need anything. (with not)
There is nothing on the list. (no not)

A person:
Someone is at the desk.
Is anyone free at four?
I didn't see anyone.
Everyone on my shift is new.

One not, never two:
No: I don't have nothing.
Yes: I don't have anything.
Yes: I have nothing.

These words take the he and she form:
Everyone knows the list.
Something goes wrong every week.
Nothing happens before eight.
grammar.workedExample:
Is there ___ for me to do? (something / anything)
1. Look at the end of the line. It is a question.
2. In a question, use anything.
3. Is there anything for me to do?
4. Now answer it two ways.
5. Yes, there is something. Or: No, there is nothing.
grammar.commonMistake:
Two nots in one line is easy to write and hard to hear.
No: I didn't say nothing.
Yes: I didn't say anything.
Yes: I said nothing.
Count the nots in the line. One is enough.
grammar.memoryTip: Plain sentence: some. Question or not: any. Nothing means not a thing.

grammar.answerKey:
1. something  2. anything  3. nothing  4. Everyone  5. anyone  6. anything  7. Someone  8. goes
Wrong on 2 or 5? A question takes any.
Wrong on 3 or 6? Line 6 already has not, so it needs anything.
Wrong on 8? These words take the he and she form.
7 or 8 right: good. 5 or less: read the card again.

grammar.title: What is it like? What is it about?
grammar.explanation:
Like asks you to describe a thing. What is it like? It is quiet.
About names the subject. What is it about? It is about money.
The two questions want two different kinds of answer.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Like asks: describe it.
What is your new job like?
It is stressful, but it is worth it.
What is the training like?
It is long and a little boring.

Like here is not the same as I like tea.
No: What is it like? I like it.

About names the subject.
What is the book about?
It is about money.
The email is about my wage.
We talked about the deadline.

Two questions, two answers:
What is it like? Tiring.
What is it about? Overtime.
grammar.workedExample:
A colleague asks: What is your shift like?
1. Like asks you to describe the shift.
2. So answer with describing words.
3. Not with a time, and not with a subject.
4. It is long and quiet.
5. Now the other one: What is the notice about? It is about training.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to answer a like question with I like.
No: What is your job like? I like it.
Yes: What is your job like? It is busy but normal.
Like in the question means describe it.
grammar.memoryTip: Like: describe it. About: name the subject.

7. She wrote to me ___ my wage.
8. What is your class ___? Is it quiet?
grammar.answerKey:
1. like  2. about  3. about  4. like  5. about  6. like  7. about  8. like
Can you answer with quiet, boring or stressful? Then it is like.
Can you answer with a subject, such as money or customers? Then it is about.

grammar.title: I need to go. I finish working.
grammar.explanation:
Some words take to and a plain word: I need to go.
Some words take a word with ing: I finish working.
The first word decides. The list is short, so learn the two groups.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Takes to:
need — I need to prepare the room.
want — I want to apply.
hope — I hope to start on Monday.
plan — We plan to arrange it today.
decide — She decides to attend.
learn — I am learning to handle customers.

Takes ing:
finish — I finish working at eight.
enjoy — I enjoy training new staff.
keep — He keeps asking me.
avoid — I avoid working on Sunday.
practise — I practise speaking every day.

Takes both, same meaning:
continue — It continues to rain. It continues raining.
like — I like to cook. I like cooking.

After to, the word keeps no ending:
No: I need to going.
Yes: I need to go.
grammar.workedExample:
I finished ___ the room at six. (prepare)
1. Find the first word: finished.
2. Finish is in the ing group.
3. So prepare takes ing: preparing.
4. I finished preparing the room at six.
5. Test it: I finished to prepare sounds wrong. Good.
grammar.commonMistake:
After to, the second word keeps no ending.
No: I need to going now.
Yes: I need to go now.
No: I enjoy to train new staff.
Yes: I enjoy training new staff.
Look at the first word. That word decides, not the second one.
grammar.memoryTip: need, want, plan: to. finish, enjoy, keep, avoid: ing.

4. He finished ___ the boxes at four. (organise)
5. I want ___ for the manager's job. (apply)
6. Keep ___ the customer's name. (say)
7. She decided ___ the training. (attend)
8. I avoid ___ overtime on Friday. (do)
grammar.answerKey:
1. to handle  2. working  3. to train  4. organising  5. to apply  6. saying  7. to attend  8. doing
Need, plan, want and decide take to: 1, 3, 5 and 7.
Enjoy, finish, keep and avoid take ing: 2, 4, 6 and 8.
Wrong on 4? Organise loses its e: organising.
7 or 8 right: good. 5 or less: read the two lists again.

teacherNotes.note: Every card shows one item done before its practice, every exercise has a key with a score line, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back and a short checklist. If you are helping, listen to the recording together and point at the checklist rather than correcting mid-sentence. Nothing in the unit needs a second person.

teacherNotes.sourceFile: Grade 3 Unit 3, Grade 3 Unit 5; Grade 4 Unit 1
teacherNotes.noteType: The one error worth your attention
teacherNotes.note: The ending after he, she and it is the error learners keep making long after they know the rule: she do, he have. Listen for it in Speaking 2 and look for it in Writing 2. Point at the word at the front of the line and let the learner fix the end themselves. The second error here is two nots in one sentence: I did not say nothing. Point at the not that is already there, then ask for the two correct versions.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.sourceFile: Grade 3 Unit 3, Grade 3 Unit 5; Grade 4 Unit 1
teacherNotes.note: No task assumes a job, a car, a home, papers or children. Every task about work offers the other side, 'or where you study', and every task about the learner's own week says it can be made up. A made-up week practises the language exactly as well as a true one; never ask whether it is real. No task asks for a real wage, a real address or any other real personal detail.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.sourceFile: Grade 3 Unit 3, Grade 3 Unit 5; Grade 4 Unit 1
teacherNotes.noteType: What is and is not taught here
teacherNotes.note: The plain -s after he, she and it was taught in Level 1 Unit 14 and is used freely. This unit adds only the forms you cannot work out — does, has, goes — with the es and ies spellings beside them. Verb plus to and verb plus -ing began in Level 1 Unit 19 with hope and enjoy; here it is a wider list sorted into two groups, plus continue, which takes both with no change of meaning. Some, any and no as quantifiers were Level 1 Unit 17; the pronouns something, anyone and everyone are new. Tag questions, would you like, the present perfect and reported speech belong to later units — leave them out.

teacherNotes.sourceFile: Grade 3 Unit 3, Grade 3 Unit 5; Grade 4 Unit 1
teacherNotes.note: The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner, not a marking service, and no task here is scored by it alone: every practice carries its own key and every recording carries its own checklist. Keep the wording that invites a made-up name, a made-up colleague and a made-up week, and never ask the learner to give the tutor real details about their home, their money or their hours.
